description.narrative:
Naguru Teenage Information and Health Center (NTIHC) har sökt finansiellt stöd från Sverige motsvarande MSEK 38.2 med syfte att implementera sin 2015-2020 strategiska plan. NTIHC kommer inte att vidarebefordra finansiella medel i tredje led.
Målet med insatsen är att öka förståelse för sexuell och reproduktiv hälsa och rättigheter (SRHR) samt tillgång till ungdomsanpassade SRH tjänster. Tre resultat har identifierats för att bidra till måluppfyllelsen:
1) Fullskalig service: Att erbjuda högkvalitativa ungdomsanpassade SRH tjänster på Kiswa ungdomsklinik och på omkringliggande hälsokliniker och att dela evidensbaserade erfarenheter bland personal genom att erbjuda dem möjlighet till praktisk inlärning. 2) Utöka tjänster: Att utöka och förbättra ungdomsanpassade SRH tjänster på ett urval offentliga primärvårdskliniker genom att tillhandahålla material och tekniskt stöd 3) Förespråka ungdomars fullständiga SRH rättigheter: Att öka medvetenhet och insikt om, samt förståelse och acceptans av, unga människors SRHR och att bygga en accepterande miljö för unga människors fullständiga SRH rättigheter.
Den totala strategibudgeten uppgår till MSEK 45.5. Av detta kommer hälsoministeriet, KCCA, Ugandas Röda Kors via UNFPA, Information Centret för AIDS och CHAU att sammanlagt tillhandahålla MSEK 7.3. NTIHC har ansökt om resterande belopp motsvarande MSEK 38.2 från Sverige.
Sverige har också finansierat NTIHCs strategiska plan 2011-2016, under perioden 2011-2014 och med en kostnadsförlängning från juli 2014- juni 2015.

Naguru Teenage Information and Health Center (NTIHC) has applied to Sweden for funding of 38.2 MSEK to implement its 2015-2020 Strategic Plan. NTIHC will not forward funds to third parties.
The intervention aims at increasing the understanding of sexual and reproductive health (SRH) rights and access to appropriate youth-friendly services for young people through three strategic objectives: 1) Best practice: To provide excellent youth friendly SRH services at Kiswa health center and in the surrounding community, and share best practices with practitioners by providing them with practical learning opportunities. 2) Scale up: To expand and improve youth friendly SRH services in selected public health facilities by providing material and technical support. 3) Promote ASRHR: To increase awareness, understanding and acceptance of young people’s SRH rights and advocate for a more enabling environment for ASRHR.
The intervention’s total budget is 45.5 MSEK, out of which 7.3 MSEK will be funded by Ministry of Health, KCCA, Uganda Red Cross Society through UNFPA, AIDS Information Center and CHAU. NTIHC has requested Sweden to fund the remaining MSEK 38.2.
Sweden has also provided support to NTIHC’s current five year Strategic Plan (2011/2012 – 2015/2016) for the period 2011-2014, with a cost extension to June 2015.

The thematic focus for the contribution is sexual and reproductive health and rights for young people.
The intended outcome is an increased understanding of sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) and access to appropriate youth-friendly services for young people in Uganda.
The overall goal of Naguru Teenage Information & Health Centre (NTIHC) strategic plan is to increase understanding of Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) and access to appropriate youth friendly services for young people. This goal is to be achieved through 3 specific objectives:
Objective 1: Best practice. To provide excellent youth friendly SRH services at Kiswa Health Centre and in the surrounding community, and share best practices with practitioners by providing them with practical learning opportunities. Under this objective, NTIHC positions itself as a best practice centre for Adolescent Sexual & Reproductive Health & Rights (ASRHR) services in Uganda and the region.
Objective 2: Scale up. To expand and improve youth friendly SRH services in selected public health facilities by providing material and technical support. This objective focus on scaling up ASRHR services beyond Kampala.
Objective 3: Promote ASRHR. To increase awareness, understanding and acceptance of young people's SRH rights and advocate for a more enabling environment for ASRHR. Objective 3 is central for increasing knowledge and awareness of SRHR, empowering young people to demand for better services as well as holding duty bearers accountable for delivery of quality services and to promote/protecting SRHR of young people in Uganda.

Overall, this support has contributed to a significant increase in Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) services utilization and understanding of SRH rights among young people in the central region where NTIHC have implemented most of its activities. In total, the NTHIC have implemented activities in 9 districts in the central region of Uganda and 6 districts in Eastern Uganda, more specifically the Bukedi Subregion. Across the region, 31 health facilities have been supported continuously throughout implementation.
The following analysis is based on the final narrative report and final evaluation report from Naguru Teenage Information and Health Centre (NTIHC), written in 2020 and 2021 respectively, covering the implementation period between 2015 and 2020.
Summary of Key Results:
NTIHC summarizes the main achievements from the implementation period, starting in 2015, along the following lines:
- Approximately 1.8 million young people accessed SRHR services across all facilities supported by the NTIHC program, representing 42 percent of all the 2.9 million young people that were projected to live in the targeted area, according to the Uganda Bureau of Statistics (UBOS).
- Overall, 185.700 cases of young people visited NTIHC Kiswa, which was consistent through the Strategy Plan (SP) implementation period. Throughout, client satisfaction was high (95%).
- On average, 21.457 young people utilized services per facility in 2019/2020 compared to the figure of 12.708 from 2015/16.
- From 2015/16 to 2019/20, service utilization increased by roughly 8.085 young people per facility from 17.925 to 26.010. Mainly, this occurred after a change in delivery where these young people, due to this intervention, could access services through Services Delivery (SD) package of support.
- A total of 1.475 peer educators and health workers were involved in service delivery and members of civil society organizations were given tailored training in youth friendly services (YFS) and ASRHR,
- On a negative note, capacity building (CB) health facilities services utilization decreased from approximately 5.217 young people per facility in 2015/16 to 4.463 in 2019/20. Mainly, this decrease has been attributed to chronic shortage of drugs and long waiting time in certain facilities.
- As a part of this contribution, the understanding of SRH rights increased from 20% in 2015 when a baseline was conducted to 74% in 2020 at the end-term evaluation.
Concerning objective 1 of best practices, activities have been focusing towards offering quality SRH services to young people in Kiswa and its surrounding communities. Predominantly, the center in Kiswa have offered a comprehensive package of SRH services, organized in 4 broad categories being: HIV Testing Services (HTS); Sexually Transmitting Infections/Disease (STI/STD) diagnosis and treatment; Maternal Health Services; and General Medical Care. During the five years of implementation, 185.700 young people accessed services at NTIHC with 63% of these being female. Totally, 131.847 young people (71%) received these services at the facility while the remaining 53.853 people gained access through a community-based approach. This community-based approach targeted young people who risked missing out on these services due to their inability to visit the centers. However, it should be noted that the program recorded a shortage of 4% of the overall target of 193.922 for the 5-year implementation period. Mainly, this shortage has been attributed to the outbreak of the Covid-19 pandemic, which severely affected the last 3 months of implementation.
Overall, the NTIHC have demonstrated best practices within SRHR through sustained quality of services, evidenced by over 80% client satisfaction regarding received services. Alongside, since the inception of antiretroviral therapy (ART) services in 2017, NTIHC have successfully retained HIV/AIDS clients enrolled on ART where nearly 98% remained active on treatment. The community-based approach also assisted in reaching the most-at-risk populations (MARPs), especially vulnerable youth populations. Finally, another great achievement related to objective 1, was the training of staff, generating staff performance competitiveness, productivity, and competence.
With regard for objective 2 scale up, it was principally implemented through 2 packages of support: (1) service delivery package to help health facilities provide care and treatment alongside creating awareness of SRHR and (2) capacity building package of support, to help public health facilities integrate Youth Friendly Service (YFS) program in the facilities. Totally, the NTIHC worked to integrate and strengthen YFS delivery in 31 public health facilities in districts across the central region of Uganda. Additionally, NTIHC contributed in training 580 health workers and 630 peer educators from a broad spectrum of public and private health facilities and Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) in the region.
Throughout the entirety of the program, service utilization increased annually. In 2015/16, 16.730 young people per facility accessed SD and CB services, compared to 29.725 young people in 2019/20. Also, through the training of health workers and peer educators, NTIHC has sustained Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health Rights (ASRHR) service delivery in public health facilities making direct improvement in health-seeking behaviors among young people. Furthermore, the work of NTIHC have been fundamental in fostering integration between YFS in private facilities, including private-not-for-profit (PNFP) programs, facilitating expansion of YFS activities.
Concerning objective 3 of promoting ASRHR, priority has been directed towards the part of the population previously not being aware of SRHR, the majority being adolescents and young people. From a baseline study in 2015, conducted by NTIHC in 16 districts, only 27 percent of all adolescents and 42 percent of the overall population could briefly mention 3 of the SRH rights listed by International Planned Parenthood Federation (IPPF). However, through the implementation of this program, NTIHC have achieved significant changes in the SRHR landscape in Uganda, contributing to policy advocacy at both national and local levels.
For instance, through intense awareness-raising sessions, NTIHC have contributed to a massive increment in understanding SRHR among the general population. In 2020, 94 percent of the overall population stated that they had an improved knowledge of their SRHR, compared to 42 percent in 2015. Mainly, this outcome has been generated due to the sensitization of communities on SRHR issues; engaging young people in improving health seeking behaviors and practices. Alongside, 600 health workers and 700 peer educators have been trained in public health facilities, enhancing the capacity of health systems to deliver improved SRHR services across Uganda. Additionally, the work of NTIHC have provided learning opportunities for others through conferences, research, and the demonstration of good practices, which have stimulated the expansion of YFS.
Rather on an overarching level, the NTIHC have contributed to the following four outcomes:
1. Increased knowledge and understanding of SRHR among young people in Uganda with these populations showing tendencies of improved health-seeking behaviors and practices, together with changing attitudes towards health care providers.
2. Sustained quality of SRH services at NTIHC with more than 75 percent of its services meeting the recommended quality standards of the Ministry of Health (MoH), generating an increased client satisfaction
3. Functionalized District Committees on Adolescent Health (DICAH), being institutionalized into local government activities.
4. Improved SRHR Landscape (policies and service delivery), which have informed a number of policy development processes.
